summary:
Beyond the Horizon: First Light is a browser-based lunar mission trainer for the 2026 challenge "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer". The player wakes as the only astronaut at a damaged south-pole outpost and has eight simulated days  to restore power and life support, build a radiation shelter, and survive a solar particle event whose start time cannot be predicted.

Under the game is a working simulation: a battery and solar power budget that follows the site's sunlit and dark spells, cabin oxygen, CO2, pressure and temperature, an EVA suit with limited oxygen and battery, and a radiation dose model in which shielding changes the result. Players learn by making real trade-offs. They can see why the lights go out, what happens to CO2 when the scrubber loses power, and how much a shelter actually reduces their dose.

The trainer matters because it teaches how astronauts reason about the risks on future Artemis-era surface missions, not just isolated facts. Key numbers on the HUD and in Mission Control (14 live values, such as battery, CO2 and dose) can be opened  to show its formula, its unit, its source and an honest evidence label: Observed, Modelled, Estimated, Game Abstraction, Authored or Fictional. Players learn to tell a real NASA reference value from a gameplay value. The game runs offline in any modern browser, needs no install or account, and includes a Simple mode for younger players. MIRA, an in-game mission assistant, tells the player what to do next.
details:
What it does

Beyond the Horizon: First Light is a single-player lunar survival trainer. The player is an astronaut who arrives at a crippled outpost near the lunar south pole. The mission is a fixed 192-hour clock (32 steps of 6 hours) divided into eight story phases: The Awakening, Choose Your Ground, Establish the Outpost, Breath of Life, The Unknown, The Warning, Engineering Under Pressure, and Mission Debrief. To win, the player must keep the crew alive, build enough power to get through the dark spells, construct a radiation shelter (8 crew-hours of work), and be inside it when a solar particle event arrives. In Full mode the cabin leak must also be repaired. The forecast gives only a risk window, never an exact start time, because, as NASA's radiation guidance notes, solar particle events cannot be reliably predicted.

There are two modes:

- Simple mode (the default, for younger or newer players) has three clear jobs: build power, build the shelter, and survive the storm.

- Full mode adds engineering faults: a damaged power distribution unit (PDU-01) with a guided circuit repair, a cabin pressure leak that must be found by inspection and then repaired and verified, a second faulty circuit, and prediction quizzes in which the player forecasts what the simulation will do before it happens.

Players explore the outpost and surrounding terrain on foot with a suited, animated astronaut under one-sixth gravity. They scavenge parts from a wrecked lander and rover, install solar strings and battery modules, manage cabin systems, and plan EVAs within the suit's oxygen, CO2 and battery limits, keeping enough in reserve to walk back.

How it works

The game runs on a deterministic, step-based simulation engine (power, life support, thermal, radiation, EVA, outpost construction and fault models) that updates once per simulated hour:

- Power: solar output follows the site's illumination profile through its sunlit and dark spells. A battery with charge and discharge efficiency and an emergency reserve supplies the loads. Loads are shed by priority when energy runs short.

- Life support: cabin O2 and CO2 are tracked as separate gases using the ideal gas law and molar masses. They come from crew metabolic rates (0.59 g/min O2 used and 0.69 g/min CO2 produced, from the NASA ICES-2021 metabolic profile paper), an electrolyser, a CO2 scrubber and a water ledger with about 90% recovery (the ISS figure from NASA's ECLSS page).

- Thermal: a heat balance between heater power, crew heat, habitat heat loss to a lit or dark sink, and heat rejection.

- Radiation: cumulative dose is the sum of dose rate times time. A solar particle event adds a large dose over a few steps, and the hull wall and the shelter multiply the rate down. The shielding direction follows NASA's radiation protection technical brief (OCHMO, NASA-STD-3001): shielding cuts solar-event dose a lot and cosmic-ray dose only a little.

- EVA: an 8-hour maximum and a walking pace of about 2 km/h, from a NASA exploration EVA analogue testing document.

An end-of-mission gate checks life support, and a debrief turns the run into a Mission Record: score, achievements, (in Full mode) forecast versus what was observed, and what the player could improve.

Educational design

- DO THIS NEXT and MIRA: a mission assistant (offline and scripted by default) always shows the next sensible action, explains why, and answers questions from a built-in knowledge base.

- Explain This Number: click a value (battery, CO2, dose and others) to see its formula, its variables and units, its live value, what high or low means, and where the number comes from.

- Formula Book (Full mode): all 67 simulation parameters with ID, value, unit, evidence label and source note.

- Evidence labels throughout: Observed, Modelled, Estimated, Game Abstraction, Authored, Fictional. The game says openly that, for example, the 600 mSv solar event is an authored scenario, not a forecast, and that its 250 mSv threshold is a gameplay reference, not a real safety limit.

- Predict, then observe: Full mode asks players to predict outcomes before the simulation shows them.

Benefits

It turns abstract space-science ideas (energy budgets, the difference between O2 and CO2, cumulative dose versus dose rate, shielding, sunlit and dark spells at the lunar south pole, risk under uncertainty) into decisions that have visible consequences. It is free, has no install and no account, works offline, and runs in a browser on laptops and touch devices, so it can be used in classrooms with poor connectivity. Its honesty about evidence is itself a lesson in scientific literacy.

What we hope to achieve

We want young people to feel what mission planning is like: limited resources, incomplete information and trade-offs, where good engineering habits (measure, predict, verify) keep a crew alive. Next steps are more NASA terrain and illumination data for real candidate sites, classroom lesson plans, and an optional multiplayer crew mode.

Tools and technologies

HTML5, CSS and plain JavaScript (60 source modules bundled into one script). Rendering uses Canvas 2D with pixel-art sprites, and audio is synthesised procedurally with the Web Audio API, with optional speech-synthesis voice. The game has no third-party runtime libraries and uses only system fonts, so it runs fully offline from the game folder or from a one-file build. The optional MIRA API is TypeScript on Node.js with Express, Zod and an optional Google Gemini call for rewording, whose answers are checked against the game's own numbers. The game never needs it. Testing uses Node.js with Playwright-core: an automated playtest bot that plays complete missions with 11 strategies, plus unit, scenario and UI checks, and Vitest for the API. AI coding assistants were used during development (see "Use of Super Intelligence").
